title: Does BPP differ from BQP?
formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language L⊆{0,1}* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time C(n+1)^k on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most 1/3 separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on 1ⁿ generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |x⟩, polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |0⟩, and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least 2/3 for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
answer_criterion: Prove BPP≠BQP or prove BPP=BQP. Since classical randomized computation can be simulated efficiently by quantum computation, a separation requires a BQP language outside BPP. An exponential oracle-query separation, a sampling separation, or a classical lower bound confined to bounded depth does not by itself provide that language.
context:
Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality BPP=BQP would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.
why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.

importance.reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.

title: Does P equal NP?
formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability.
answer_criterion: Prove P=NP or P≠NP. A polynomial-time SAT algorithm settles the equality direction. For separation, prove that some language in NP has no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm; equivalently, rule out every such algorithm for SAT. Failure of a particular search procedure or a lower bound for a restricted circuit model does not establish that separation.
context:
A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. P=NP would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. P≠NP would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. They guide the search for new arguments; they are not proofs that the problem is unsolvable.
why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

importance.reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove P≠NP.
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

title: Does P equal PSPACE?
formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most C(n+1)^k work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form Q₁x₁⋯Qₘxₘ φ(x₁,…,xₘ), where each Qᵢ is ∃ or ∀, quantified variables are distinct, and φ is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over {0,1}. The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove P=PSPACE or P≠PSPACE. A polynomial-time TQBF decider proves equality. To prove separation, exhibit one PSPACE language that has no polynomial-time algorithm, equivalently rule out every polynomial-time TQBF decider. A lower bound against only one fixed polynomial time exponent is insufficient.
context:
Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. A full winning strategy may have exponentially many branches, although each play has polynomial length. The characterization of polynomial space by polynomial-time alternation explains why many polynomial-length planning and game problems are PSPACE-complete.

The inclusion P⊆PSPACE is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. P≠NP would imply P≠PSPACE because NP⊆PSPACE. A proof of P=NP, however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem IP=PSPACE characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance toward time lower bounds. A multitape computation taking t steps can be simulated in O(sqrt(t log t)) space. Combined with the space hierarchy, this excludes near-quadratic time bounds for some linear-space problems. The exponent is still fixed: it does not give a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.
why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

importance.reason: A defining question about the relationship between the two basic computational resources, time and working memory. It is a top-priority foundational class separation.

progress.text: Quantified Boolean formulas provide a PSPACE-complete target. Chandra, Kozen, and Stockmeyer characterize deterministic polynomial space as alternating polynomial time.
Shamir proves IP=PSPACE, giving an interactive-proof characterization without resolving deterministic polynomial-time computation.
Williams proves the O(sqrt(t log t)) space simulation of time-t multitape machines, improving the decades-old O(t/log t) bound. It yields fixed-exponent time lower bounds for linear-space languages.

title: Is the polynomial hierarchy strict at every finite level?
formal: Is $\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}$ for every integer k≥0? Here Σ₀^P=P, and Σₖ^P for k≥1 consists of languages definable by k alternating blocks of polynomially bounded Boolean quantifiers, beginning existentially, followed by a deterministic polynomial-time predicate.
definitions: A language L is in Σₖ^P if there exist a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R such that, for every binary input x, $x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1$, where Qₖ is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Each yᵢ is an entire string, so k counts quantifier blocks, not individual bits. The predicate is polynomial-time in the combined input length. k is fixed for a class membership claim and cannot grow with |x|; p and R may depend on k and L. Let Πₖ^P consist of complements of Σₖ^P languages, and let PH=⋃ₖ≥0Σₖ^P. In particular Σ₁^P=NP and Π₁^P=coNP. These are uniform, unrelativized classes of total decision languages. Strictness at level k means that some language in Σₖ₊₁^P is absent from Σₖ^P. The separating language may depend on k. All classes use ordinary Turing computation with no advice or external oracle.
answer_criterion: Prove strict containment at every finite level, or prove equality Σₖ^P=Σₖ₊₁^P for some fixed k. Equality at any adjacent pair collapses all higher levels to that level, so a collapse at even one finite level answers no. Proving strictness for finitely many levels or relative to an oracle does not answer yes.
context:
NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because unused quantifier blocks can be inserted. Its collapse property is much stronger: if two neighboring levels coincide, all later alternations can be eliminated down to that level. Consequently the target is a single binary statement, not a request to classify an unspecified collection of logical formulas.

Strictness includes P≠NP at its first step, but P≠NP alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.
why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.

progress.text: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy; Stockmeyer develops its structural properties and complete problems.
Oracle constructions show that all levels can be distinct in a relativized world. Karp–Lipton-type theorems connect small circuits for NP to a collapse of the unrelativized hierarchy.
Rossman, Servedio, and Tan establish infinitude relative to a random oracle with probability one. Their proof comes from an average-case lower bound separating consecutive constant circuit depths.

Hirsch and Volkovich study the Linear Ordering Principle, related small complexity classes, and Karp–Lipton-style conditional collapses. These are implications under hypotheses, not an unconditional collapse or separation of PH.

title: Does NP contain a language without polynomial-size Boolean circuits?
formal: Is $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}$? Precisely, does there exist one language L∈NP such that, for every integer k≥1, real C>0, and integer N≥1, some n≥N satisfies $\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k$, where Lₙ is the characteristic function of L on n-bit inputs and CC is minimum Boolean circuit size?
definitions: A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n input bits, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants 0 and 1, and one output bit. There are no depth or fan-out restrictions; a gate output may be reused arbitrarily. Size counts AND, OR, and NOT gates. Lₙ must be computed exactly on every n-bit string. A family {Cₙ} is nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct Cₙ from n, and the circuit may depend arbitrarily on the input length, but not on the particular input of that length. P/poly consists of languages having circuits of size at most C(n+1)^k for some fixed constants C,k and every n. NP consists of languages L with a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p such that x∈L iff some y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. The existentially chosen language L is the same for every exponent k. The lower bound need only hold at arbitrarily large lengths for each k; an eventual bound at every sufficiently large length would be stronger. Equivalently, ask whether the NP-complete language SAT has no polynomial-size circuit family under an ordinary explicit binary formula encoding.
answer_criterion: Prove NP is not contained in P/poly, or prove the containment. A positive separation requires one NP language escaping every polynomial circuit-size bound. Proving that, for each exponent k, a possibly different language requires more than n^k gates does not suffice. Containment can be established by giving polynomial-size circuits for SAT at every input length; an efficient uniform circuit generator is not required.
context:
A polynomial-time algorithm yields a polynomial-size circuit for each input length by unrolling its computation. The converse fails because a different circuit may be selected for every length without any effective way to generate those circuits. The conjecture asks whether NP retains hard problems even after granting this substantial extra freedom. A separation would imply P≠NP, while P≠NP alone does not establish the circuit claim.

Counting arguments show that most truth tables need exponentially many gates. They do not produce the required language in NP: an arbitrary sequence of hard truth tables need not have efficiently verifiable membership certificates. This is the central explicitness difficulty. It is also why enumerating hard functions at a few fixed lengths cannot satisfy the quantified statement on this card.

The Karp–Lipton theorem gives a consequence of the opposite outcome: if NP has polynomial-size circuits, the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level. This is evidence linking nonuniform algorithms to uniform complexity, but it is not a contradiction because the hierarchy is not known to be infinite.

Under sufficiently strong pseudorandom-function assumptions, a property of truth tables that is both efficiently recognizable and sufficiently common cannot distinguish all hard functions from polynomial-size circuits in the required way. title: Can every polynomial-time decision problem be solved in logarithmic space?
formal: Is L=P? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses O(log(n+2)) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most C log₂(n+2) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in O((n+2)ᶜ) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth.
answer_criterion: Answer yes by giving a logarithmic-workspace decider for Circuit Value or otherwise proving P⊆L. Answer no by proving that some fixed language in P has no O(log n)-space deterministic decider. A lower bound on memory used by one evaluation strategy, or on algorithms with an extra time restriction, does not rule out all of L.
context:
A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A small-space algorithm may instead recompute information when it is needed. The question asks whether this tradeoff can always reduce working memory to a constant number of input indices and counters. The input remains available for repeated reading, so this is a different model from a single-pass streaming algorithm.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

L⊆NL⊆P, where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that L≠NL would therefore separate L from P, but L=NL would not itself settle L=P. Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Williams simulates time t in O(√(t log t)) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller O(log n) target unresolved.

title: Does every unsatisfiable Boolean formula have a short efficiently checkable certificate?
formal: Do there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a fixed polynomial p such that, for every Boolean CNF formula F, $F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\iff\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|F|)}:V(F,\pi)=1$, with V never accepting a certificate for a satisfiable formula? Equivalently, is NP=coNP? The verification algorithm and polynomial are fixed for all formulas.
definitions: A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals x or NOT x. Variables take values in {0,1}; unsatisfiable means that no assignment makes all clauses true. The formula is encoded explicitly in binary, and |F| is its total bit length, including variable names and all literal occurrences. Empty clauses and an empty conjunction have their usual false and true meanings. V halts in time polynomial in |F|+|pi| on every pair of strings and rejects malformed formula encodings. Certificates may be arbitrary binary strings; they are not restricted to any particular inference calculus. NP is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked in deterministic polynomial time. coNP consists of complements of NP languages. No randomization, oracle, advice, or interaction with a prover is allowed.
answer_criterion: Construct a sound verifier and one polynomial length bound covering every unsatisfiable formula, or prove that no such verifier and bound exist. Equivalently, prove NP=coNP or NP≠coNP. A lower bound for a particular proof system is insufficient for separation, and an efficient algorithm for finding certificates is not required for equality.
context:
A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when NP=coNP. The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.
why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.

importance.reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between NP=coNP and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. This turns a complexity-class question into a precise proof-length target.

The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.

title: Can directed reachability be decided in deterministic logarithmic space?
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices {1,...,n} and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to L=NL.
definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so s=t is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic O(log N) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has N=Theta(n^2) bits, O(log N)=O(log n). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
context:
A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within n−1 edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses O(log² n) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, NL=coNL shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.
why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

importance.reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in O(s²) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an O(log² n)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular NL=coNL, so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.

title: Does P≠NP imply the existence of one-way functions?
formal: Does P≠NP imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant c>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
definitions: Uₙ is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output f(x), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real c>0 there exists N(I,c) such that the inequality holds for every n≥N(I,c). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise P≠NP concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.
answer_criterion: Prove or disprove the implication under the stated classical uniform security definition. A positive answer must obtain an eventually secure one-way function from P≠NP alone, without assuming average-case hardness, factoring hardness, or a separate derandomization hypothesis. An oracle separation or a lower bound for a restricted kind of reduction only limits that proof approach; it does not disprove the unrelativized implication.
context:
If P=NP, an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.
why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

importance.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.

title: Can randomness always be removed from polynomial-time decision algorithms?
formal: Does P=BPP? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
definitions: Input length is n=|x|. A polynomial-time bound means C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
answer_criterion: Prove that every BPP language has a deterministic polynomial-time decider, or exhibit a BPP language and prove that none exists. A subexponential simulation, a simulation using advice, or correctness only on most inputs does not settle the question. Proving the stronger derandomization claim for all promise problems would suffice, but is not required here.
context:
Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

One simple approach is to run the randomized algorithm on every possible random tape and take the majority answer. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely P≠NP. Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.
why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

importance.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

progress.text: Adleman establishes BPP⊆P/poly. Suitable fixed random advice exists for each input length, but uniform polynomial-time computation of that advice is not supplied.

title: Do some tautologies require superpolynomial Extended Frege proofs?
formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants C>0 and c≥1, is there a propositional tautology φ whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than C(|φ|+2)ᶜ? Here |φ| is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
definitions: Fix Boolean formulas over ¬ and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), together with modus ponens from A and A→B to B. An Extended Frege proof of φ may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms e→θ and θ→e. Here e is fresh, absent from φ, θ, and every preceding line; θ uses original variables of φ and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be φ, with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness.
answer_criterion: Answer yes by proving that no single polynomial bounds the shortest EF proof of every tautology. Answer no by establishing constants C,c that bound the shortest proof of every tautology by C(|φ|+2)ᶜ. The yes direction does not require that the hard tautologies be generated in polynomial time. A lower bound for an algorithm that searches for proofs, or for a restricted subsystem, is not a lower bound on all EF proofs.
context:
Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If NP≠coNP, every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of NP≠coNP.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to P≠NP under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.
why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize propositional proof systems, polynomial simulation, and Extended Frege, proving robustness under the choice of standard rules and connectives.
Strong lower bounds emerge for weaker systems, while even unrestricted Frege lower bounds remain open. EF adds the ability to abbreviate and share formulas.

Pich and Santhanam establish conditional routes from EF proof lower bounds to P≠NP. The assumptions include formally provable computational statements; the result is not an unconditional EF lower bound.
Hsieh, Jain, Li, and Mathialagan obtain SNARGs for NP from derandomization, LWE, SXDH, and a bounded-arithmetic unprovability assumption concerning certificates of EF-hard tautologies.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations in extended polynomial calculus with a square-root rule. Its Section 1 explicitly distinguishes this from propositional Frege and EF lower bounds.

title: Is the matrix multiplication exponent equal to two?
formal: Fix the field of complex numbers. Let s(n) be the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit that computes all entries of AB exactly for arbitrary n-by-n matrices A,B. Is it true that $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists C_\varepsilon>0\;\forall n\ge2:\ s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}$? Equivalently, is $\omega=\inf\{\tau:s(n)=O(n^\tau)\}=2$?
definitions: The inputs are 2n² independent complex variables a_ij,b_ij. The required n² output polynomials are c_ij=sum_{k=1}^n a_ik b_kj. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for every fixed positive epsilon, or prove omega>2. For the negative direction, it suffices to show that for some fixed epsilon>0 no constant C bounds s(n) by C n^(2+epsilon) for all n. A fixed improvement such as omega<2.37 is progress but not a resolution. Equality of the infimum does not require an O(n²) circuit family or an O(n² polylog n) bound.
context:
The usual algorithm computes n² inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.

The question is whether one can keep reducing the extra exponent all the way to zero. Its quantifiers matter. An algorithm for each exponent 2+epsilon is enough, even when its constant depends badly on epsilon. Conversely, improving one decimal place in the current upper bound does not establish the conjecture. Fixing the field and counting exact scalar operations also separates this question from approximate numerical multiplication or hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.
why: Matrix multiplication is a basic operation whose exponent enters many algorithms in linear algebra and graph theory. Determining whether its arithmetic cost can approach the quadratic scale would settle a central question about sharing computation among many related outputs.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

progress.text: Strassen gives O(n^(log₂7)) arithmetic operations, establishing that cubic multiplication is not optimal.

Alman proves that the universal method applied to any Coppersmith–Winograd tensor cannot yield an exponent below 2.16805. This is a limitation of that tensor-based route, not a proof that omega exceeds two.
The SODA paper More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication gives omega<2.371339 by extending the combination-loss analysis. The original preprint appeared in April 2024.

Dupont and coauthors report omega<2.371177. Section 4 describes rounding the optimized parameters to rationals and verifying directed bounds for logarithms; it says the verification repository is being prepared. This catalogue has not independently replayed that certificate.
Version 3 of More Asymmetry Yields Faster Matrix Multiplication incorporates the new optimization bound. The remaining gap to two persists.

title: Does the permanent have polynomial-size arithmetic circuits?
formal: Over the field $\mathbb C$, do there exist constants C,k such that, for every integer n≥1, the polynomial $\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}$ can be computed by an arithmetic circuit with at most C(n+1)^k gates? Equivalently, is $\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}$? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
definitions: X has n² independent indeterminates and S_n is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes labeled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, binary +, −, × operation gates, and one output. Its size counts operation gates; intermediate results can feed any number of later gates. Division, comparisons, oracle gates, approximation, and limits of circuits are absent. The output must equal the permanent as a formal polynomial. Circuits may depend on n without a uniform construction algorithm; constants have unit arithmetic cost, with no bit-encoding restriction. VP consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded numbers of variables and total degrees, computed by polynomial-size circuits. VNP consists of polynomial families f_n(x)=Σ_{y∈{0,1}^{p(n)}} g_n(x,y), for some polynomial p and some such polynomial-size, polynomial-degree circuit family g. The witness sum is over Boolean strings even though the coefficients lie in C.
answer_criterion: Construct the stated circuit family, or prove that the minimum circuit size of the permanent is not bounded by any polynomial in n. A lower bound for every polynomial-size general circuit family suffices. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits, or determinantal representations do not by themselves settle this formulation.
context:
The permanent sums one product for every perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph. Substituting a zero-one adjacency matrix counts perfect matchings. This card asks for an exact symbolic arithmetic computation valid on all complex matrices. The model permits cancellations and unrestricted reuse of intermediate results, so it captures substantially more than enumerating matchings.

The permanent and determinant have the same permutation products, but the determinant attaches a sign to each one. Determinants have polynomial-size division-free circuits despite their factorially many displayed terms. Thus counting the monomials in the permanent is not a circuit lower bound: the question is whether an equally effective algebraic compression exists for its unsigned sum.

Valiant makes this example universal. Every family in VNP reduces to a polynomially larger permanent by substitutions of variables and constants. A polynomial circuit for the permanent would therefore compress every efficient Boolean-witness sum in the definition of VNP. Conversely, separating these classes forces the permanent to escape polynomial circuit size.

Important partial results restrict how computations are organized. A formula cannot reuse an intermediate result; a constant-depth circuit permits only a fixed number of operation layers. Even proving that the permanent has no small determinant representation would rule out only that representation model. None of these restrictions is part of the circuit model in this card.

Recent lower bounds illustrate both the progress and the gap. Superpolynomial bounds are known at every fixed depth, and new work constructs polynomial maps that evade low-complexity parametrizations. The latter can yield stronger circuit lower bounds if its degree and dimension parameters improve sufficiently. The constructions currently cited do not give the required unrestricted superpolynomial bound.
why: This is the central separation question for arithmetic computation. It tests whether summing exponentially many efficiently describable algebraic contributions inherently requires more computation than evaluating one polynomial-size circuit, and organizes lower-bound research across algebra, geometry, and pseudorandomness.

importance.reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.

progress.text: Ryser’s inclusion-exclusion expression gives an exponential-size formula, for example O(n²2^n) arithmetic operations. This substantially improves direct enumeration of n! permutations but remains far above a polynomial bound.
Valiant establishes algebraic completeness of the permanent over fields of characteristic different from two. Over C this yields the equivalence between polynomial-size permanent circuits and VP=VNP.

Limaye, Srinivasan, and Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds against arithmetic circuits of every constant depth in characteristic zero. Those circuits may have unbounded fan-in, with size accounting for their description; the fixed depth is an essential restriction. The result does not separate general VP and VNP.

Narayanan relates elusive polynomial maps to expansion of iterated sumsets and obtains improved superlinear bounds in certain sublogarithmic-depth regimes. An explicit elusive-curve construction has exponential degree; the paper explains that its parameters do not yet imply VP≠VNP.

title: Does P≠NP imply a samplable NP problem outside AvgP?
formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove or disprove the displayed implication for ordinary Turing computation. A positive answer must derive existence of a pair (L,D) outside the precisely defined AvgP from P≠NP alone. Hardness under an arbitrary uncomputable distribution, a conjecture about one particular random-instance model, or a reduction requiring additional hardness assumptions does not establish this implication. A relativized separation only limits relativizing proof methods.
context:
Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.
why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.
